units.name: http-verbs
units.role: Give callers a one-shot way to make a single HTTP request without managing a Session.
units.description: This is the simple, well-known front door to the library: the functions people actually call, like requests.get(url) or requests.post(url, data=...). Each of these convenience functions quietly creates a short-lived session behind the scenes, sends the request through it, and closes it up afterward, so someone making one quick call doesn't have to think about managing a session themselves. It never talks to the network directly; it just translates a friendly one-line call into instructions for the more powerful session machinery that does the real work.

units.name: session
units.role: Carry state (cookies, auth, adapters, default settings) across multiple requests and drive one request's full lifecycle, including redirects.
units.description: This is the part of the library that remembers things between multiple requests to the same server, such as login cookies, saved authentication, and default settings like which proxy or headers to use — the way a browser tab remembers state across page loads. It is the main workflow that turns a description of a request ('GET this URL') into an actual exchange with a server: merging session defaults with per-call options, preparing the request, handing it to a connection adapter to actually send, following redirects, and updating the cookie jar from what came back.

units.name: request-response-model
units.role: Define what an HTTP request and an HTTP response are, independent of how bytes actually move over the wire.
units.description: This is the heart of the library: the plain-language objects that represent 'an HTTP request' and 'an HTTP response'. A Request holds what a caller asked for (method, URL, headers, body, auth); a PreparedRequest turns that into the exact wire-ready form (encoding the URL, building multipart bodies, computing content length, attaching cookies and auth); and a Response holds what came back from the server, with convenient ways to read it as raw bytes, text, JSON, or a stream of chunks. It defines what a request and a response are, independent of the transport code that actually moves bytes to and from a server.

units.name: auth-schemes
units.role: Turn credentials into the right Authorization header(s) for a request, including the Digest challenge/response protocol.
units.description: This file provides the different ways the library can prove a user's identity to a server when making a request: simple Basic Authentication, Proxy Authentication (the same idea, for a proxy server), and Digest Authentication, a back-and-forth challenge where the server first refuses a request and asks for proof of a password, hashed with a bit of randomness, without ever sending the password itself. Each scheme knows how to take credentials and add the right Authorization header to an outgoing request; Digest additionally knows how to react to a server's first '401 please authenticate' reply and resend the request with a proper answer.

units.name: exceptions
units.role: Define every kind of error and warning the library can raise when something goes wrong making a request.
units.description: This file defines every kind of error and warning that can come out of the library when something goes wrong sending an HTTP request — for example the server could not be reached, an SSL certificate failed, a URL was malformed, too many redirects happened, or a response body wasn't valid JSON. These classes are the shared vocabulary of failure that the rest of the library uses to signal problems, and that code using the library relies on to catch and handle those problems (e.g. 'catch requests.exceptions.Timeout'). It does not do anything by itself; it only names things.

units.name: transport-adapter
units.role: Actually move a prepared request over the network and turn urllib3's low-level results/errors into requests' vocabulary.
units.description: This is the part of the library that actually talks to the network. When someone makes a request, this code opens the real TCP/TLS connection to the server (via the underlying urllib3 library), sends the prepared request bytes over the wire, and turns the raw low-level response and any low-level networking errors (timeouts, broken connections, bad certificates, proxy failures) into the friendly Response objects and exception types the rest of the library understands. It also handles connection pooling and reuse, proxy configuration, and checking server certificates against a CA bundle. It doesn't know or care what the request is 'for' — only how to move it over the wire and hand back a result.

units.name: cookie-jar
units.role: Adapt Python's stdlib cookiejar into a dict-like jar and move cookies between it and requests/responses.
units.description: This code teaches the library how to store and reuse the small pieces of data called cookies that websites use to remember you (for logins, sessions, preferences). It wraps Python's built-in cookie-jar machinery so the rest of the library can treat a jar of cookies almost like a simple dictionary, and it provides the plumbing to copy cookies out of a server's response into that jar and to build the Cookie header sent on later requests. It adapts a stdlib mechanism; it doesn't encode any of the library's own request-handling logic.

units.name: http-utils
units.role: Provide small, stateless, reusable helpers (header/encoding parsing, proxy resolution, IP checks, safe file handling, CA bundle location) used throughout the library.
units.description: This is the library's shared toolbox of small, self-contained helper functions that don't belong to any single feature. It includes things like figuring out what character encoding a response is in, parsing oddly-formatted header values, deciding whether a request should go through a proxy by reading environment variables and checking IP ranges, safely writing files to disk without corrupting them if something goes wrong mid-write, and finding the bundle of trusted certificates used to verify HTTPS connections. None of these helpers tell a story about 'making an HTTP request' on their own — they are reliable, reusable building blocks that the request, session, and cookie code call into whenever they need this kind of low-level work done.

units.name: data-structures
units.role: Provide generic, domain-agnostic container types (a case-insensitive dict, an attribute-accessible lookup dict) used elsewhere.
units.description: This is a small toolbox of two generic, reusable container types that other parts of the library use to store information. CaseInsensitiveDict is a dictionary-like object that lets code look up values by key regardless of letter case (used for HTTP headers, since 'Content-Type' and 'content-type' should be treated as the same header). LookupDict is a simple dictionary variant that lets its entries be accessed like attributes (used to expose HTTP status codes as friendly names, e.g. codes.ok). Neither type talks to the network, filesystem, or clock — they are pure, self-contained building blocks that other units plug into.

units.name: hooks
units.role: Give callers a generic way to plug a callback into a request/response cycle.
units.description: This is a tiny, generic plug-in mechanism that lets other parts of the library, and people using it, hook into a request/response cycle. It defines the shape of a hooks dictionary (currently just a 'response' slot) and a function that, when a named event fires, calls any callback registered for that event and lets the callback optionally replace the data flowing through the program. It has no HTTP-specific knowledge and does no network, file, or system access of its own — it is purely a callback-dispatch utility used by the request-building and session-sending code.

units.name: compat-layer
units.role: Bootstrap the package (dependency-version checks), give the rest of the codebase one stable set of stdlib/typing names to import, and keep old import paths working.
units.description: This is the plumbing that lets the library run consistently across different Python versions, different installed dependency versions, and old code that expects an outdated import layout. One part checks that the installed urllib3 and character-detection libraries are compatible versions and warns if not, and assembles the library's public surface (the names people get from `import requests`) by importing them from wherever they're really defined. Another part resolves differences between the standard library and optional third-party replacements (like preferring simplejson over json if it's installed) so the rest of the library can rely on one set of names. A third part makes old code that imports 'requests.packages.urllib3' keep working by aliasing the real packages under that path. A fourth part is internal type-hinting support, with two small helper functions used at runtime elsewhere. None of this understands or performs HTTP requests itself; it exists so the actual HTTP logic elsewhere can run reliably everywhere.

violations_observed.note: HTTPDigestAuth.handle_401 reaches into Response/PreparedRequest internals directly (e.g. r.raw, r._cookies, r.connection) instead of going only through the listed public entrypoints (Response.close/.content/.is_redirect, PreparedRequest.copy/.prepare_cookies).
